analysis.one_liner: Rewrites retirement-savings advice rules to block the Labor Department from holding brokers to a strict best-interest standard.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee without ever getting a vote, leaving the Labor Department's new fiduciary rule on track.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change the federal pension law (ERISA) so that only advisors who sign a written fiduciary acknowledgment are held to a best-interest standard, and it would create an exemption letting advisors earn commissions and variable pay on retirement advice so long as they disclose it. It would also strip the Labor Department of its power to update investment-advice rules, and would kill the department's pending 2016 rule requiring brokers to act in savers' best interests unless Congress voted to approve it within 60 days. It never got a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Brokerage firms, insurance companies, and other financial advisers who earn commissions and variable compensation on retirement money would benefit: the bill would shield sales-based advice from fiduciary liability, let advisers sell their own proprietary products from a limited menu after a one-line notice, and block the Labor Department rule that would have required best-interest advice on IRA rollovers.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would write a narrower definition of 'investment advice' into law, so that only advisors who sign a written fiduciary acknowledgment or reach a mutual agreement with the plan are held to a best-interest standard.

It would create a new exemption from ERISA's prohibited-transaction rules allowing advisors to receive commissions and variable compensation on retirement advice, as long as compensation is 'reasonable' and disclosed with a one-sentence notice that cheaper options may exist elsewhere.

It would prohibit the Labor Department from amending any rules or administrative positions on investment advice, and would require Congress to enact a bill specifically approving the pending 2016 fiduciary rule within 60 days or the rule could never take effect.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary retirement savers, especially people rolling over 401(k) balances into IRAs, who could continue receiving advice from advisers earning commissions on the products they recommend, with higher fees potentially eroding savings over decades. Taxpayers and the Labor Department would also lose regulatory authority over the retirement-advice market.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have permanently barred the Labor Department from issuing any new rules on investment advice, including rules requiring brokers to act in savers' best interests, unless Congress specifically approved them within 60 days — a bar that would be very hard to lift in practice.

By statute it would have killed the Labor Department's pending 2016 fiduciary rule before it could take effect, since any such rule not already effective on January 1, 2015 could not become effective without a new act of Congress.

Its exemption would allow advisors to steer savers into a limited menu of proprietary products and to earn variable commissions, so long as a one-line notice is given that the same investments may be available cheaper elsewhere.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have given some legal clarity to advisers and preserved access to advice for small accounts, at the cost of blocking a rule intended to stop conflicted advice that steers retirement savers into higher-cost products. Because the bill would also have permanently barred the Labor Department from tightening investment-advice rules, its costs to savers were large and one-sided.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate HELP Committee the day it was introduced and never advanced, so it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced February 4, 2016, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action was taken — no hearings, no markup, no floor vote — and the 114th Congress ended January 3, 2017 with the bill still in committee.
Had it passed, the bill would have prohibited the Labor Department from amending investment-advice rules and required an act of Congress for the 2016 fiduciary rule to take effect.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, the Labor Department's fiduciary rule remained on track, so retirement savers kept the stronger protections it would have preempted. The bill's defeat also preserved the Labor Department's authority to regulate investment advice, while commission-based advisers did not get the statutory safe harbor they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Retirement savers; the fiduciary rule survived

for.name: Sen. Johnny Isakson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it as its lead sponsor.

for.name: Financial industry trade groups (broker-dealers, insurers, mutual fund companies)
for.role: Opponents of the DOL fiduciary rule
for.what_they_did: Publicly lobbied against the Labor Department's fiduciary rule, which this bill was designed to preempt.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, and the bill sat in committee with no Democratic support recorded.

industries.industry: Broker-dealers and financial advisers earning commissions on retirement accounts
industries.note: The bill would shield commission-based advice from fiduciary liability and create a broad exemption allowing variable compensation and sales of proprietary products, so advisers could keep selling higher-cost products to IRA and 401(k) savers. Ordinary savers bear the difference through fees.

The bill would strip the agency of authority to update investment-advice rules by regulation, requiring an act of Congress for any change — an unusual constraint on an agency charged with protecting pension participants.

Advisers already compensated only by fees would face competition from commission-based sellers who could keep selling proprietary products under the bill's new exemption, potentially at lower cost to savers but with conflicts of interest intact.
